Chapter 5: Insisting on Objective Criteria—Ensuring Fairness and Legitimacy.
You know, even when everyone means well, negotiations can still hit a wall—especially when people can't agree on what's actually fair.
If one side just tries to push their way through with pressure or power, the other person’s likely to walk away feeling resentful, maybe even a bit exploited. And deals made that way? They don’t tend to last. In fact, they can really strain relationships.
There’s a much better way to go about it—basing decisions on objective criteria. These are standards that don’t depend on what either side wants. Think of things like market value, expert opinions, legal precedents, or even what’s normal in the industry. When you do this, the conversation shifts. Suddenly it's not about “who wins,” but about “what’s actually fair.”
Picture this—two neighbors arguing over where the property line sits. If they base the discussion on what each of them prefers, things can get heated pretty fast. But if they turn to a surveyor’s map or check local zoning rules, it’s no longer personal. Now, it’s about finding a fair answer together.
So, how do you actually insist on using objective criteria? There are a few steps to keep in mind:
First, agree on what standards make sense for your situation. What measures or benchmarks are actually relevant here?
Next, be open to reason. Both sides need to explain where they're coming from and genuinely listen to each other.
Then, frame your proposals as fair and reasonable. Show how your suggestions meet those agreed-upon standards—not just what you personally want.
And here’s something crucial: never give in just to pressure. Yield only when the principle or the standard makes sense. Stay firm on using fair criteria, but be willing to talk about which standards you’ll use.
Take a salary negotiation, for example. Instead of guessing what’s fair, both the employer and the employee can look up industry salary surveys. Or in a contract dispute, both parties might pull up similar agreements from others in the field.
Now, using objective criteria doesn’t mean disagreements magically disappear. But it does give you a shared reference point. That helps everyone see the outcome as legitimate and just, and it really cuts down on resentment or backlash.
Plus, this approach protects you from power plays—things like threats or ultimatums. When both sides are committed to fairness, it becomes less about who’s stronger, and more about working together to find the best answer.
So, whenever you’re negotiating, remember: insist on objective criteria. It’s one of the most powerful ways to build trust, reach fair agreements, and preserve relationships along the way.
